blocks.text: Spectroscopy deals with producing, measuring and interpreting spectra that arise from the interaction of electromagnetic radiation with matter. A spectrum gives information about atomic and molecular energy levels, molecular shapes, interactions between molecules and the nature of chemical bonds. A spectroscopic measurement can also measure the amount of a substance in a sample (quantitative analysis) or simply identify an unknown sample (qualitative analysis).

The chemical composition of a substance can be studied with emission and absorption spectra. Each element produces a unique pattern of spectral lines, like a fingerprint, so elements can be identified by their atomic spectra. Hydrogen gives a strong red line at 656 nm; burning sodium gives a characteristic yellow flame from strong lines at 589 nm; most of mercury's emission lines are below 450 nm, giving a characteristic blue light.

blocks.title: Did you know?
blocks.text: Atomic spectra help astronomers find the chemical composition of stars: by analysing the light these bodies give out, scientists can tell which elements they contain.
